title: English Vocabulary 3 · Units 39–40
description: Curated B2 crime, criminal justice, personal banking and tax vocabulary with original examples, natural Brazilian Portuguese glosses and usage notes.
sourceNotice: Prepared from the user-supplied book for personal study. Vocabulary targets are selected from teaching pages and relevant exercises; examples and explanatory notes are newly written. The textbook passages, exercises and illustrations are not reproduced.

audit.scope: Teaching sections, terminology tables, language notes, exercises and relevant answer-key entries reviewed for meaningful lexical and grammatical coverage.
audit.pronunciation: Broad British IPA for high-confidence single words and short expressions; longer expressions may omit IPA. Regional and connected-speech variants are not exhaustively represented.
audit.languagePolicy: English only except Brazilian Portuguese glosses inside pt.
audit.reviewMethod: Manual source comparison, independent editorial review of meaning, examples, translations, prepositions and phonetic confidence, plus offline JSON schema, identifiers and audio-target checks. No live application or browser audio testing.
audit.limitations: No bundled audio is provided. Browser TTS/speech recognition and actual import into VocabLab were not tested. Legal and tax arrangements can vary between jurisdictions.

units.title: Unit 39 — Crime
units.source: Vocabulary study targets from published reference material; Unit 39. Page information, if available, is retained in sourceAudit.
units.category: Crime, investigation, court proceedings and punishment
learningObjectives: Name major crimes, their associated verbs and the people who commit them.
Distinguish suspicion, accusation, evidence, proof, conviction and acquittal.
Use criminal-justice collocations and prepositions accurately: charged with, accused of, convicted of and sentenced to.
Explain the roles of police, lawyers, judges, juries, witnesses, suspects and victims.

items.example: The police reported a fall in crime in the area.
items.note: A general word for an act that breaks criminal law; crime may also be uncountable when referring to criminal activity generally.

items.example: Detectives are investigating a murder in the city centre.
items.note: The crime of unlawfully and intentionally killing someone; it is also a verb.

items.example: The murderer was identified using evidence from the scene.
items.note: Person noun related to murder; avoid confusing murderer with victim.

items.example: The store introduced new measures to prevent shoplifting.
items.note: Taking goods from a shop without paying; a specific form of theft.

items.example: The security guard stopped a suspected shoplifter.
items.note: Person noun associated with shoplifting.

items.example: Someone tried to shoplift several expensive items.
items.note: A regular verb; past: shoplifted.

items.pt: furto em imóvel após entrada ilegal; arrombamento para furtar
items.example: A burglary was reported at the house while its owners were away.
items.note: The book describes stealing from someone's home; contrast with robbery, which involves taking property by force or threat.

items.example: The burglar entered through a back window.
items.note: The person who commits burglary.

items.pt: invadir imóvel para furtar; cometer um arrombamento
items.example: Someone attempted to burgle the flat during the night.
items.note: A regular British English verb; American English often uses burglarise.

items.example: Customs officers discovered evidence of smuggling at the port.
items.note: Secretly or illegally taking goods across borders, often avoiding customs rules.

items.example: The smuggler was stopped at the border.
items.note: Person noun associated with smuggling.

items.example: The gang attempted to smuggle goods across the frontier.
items.note: Regular verb; smuggle something into or out of a country.

items.example: Police opened an investigation into the reported kidnapping.
items.note: Taking someone against their will, sometimes to demand a ransom; it is not always motivated by money.

items.example: Investigators searched for the kidnapper after the victim escaped.
items.note: Person noun from kidnap.

items.example: They threatened to kidnap the diplomat's relative.
items.note: Regular verb; kidnapped has a doubled p.

items.example: The documentary examined the impact of terrorism on public safety.
items.note: The source describes politically motivated violence; do not confuse with terrorise, a more general verb.

items.example: The report described the suspect as an alleged terrorist.
items.note: A person involved in terrorism; allegations are not proof of guilt.

items.example: The threats were intended to terrorise local residents.
items.note: More general than the specific crime of terrorism; British spelling terrorise.

items.example: The company warned customers about online fraud.
items.note: Deceiving someone to gain money or another advantage dishonestly.

items.example: The fraudster used false documents to obtain payment.
items.note: Person noun for someone who commits fraud.

items.pt: fraudar; obter dinheiro de alguém por fraude
items.example: A dishonest employee tried to defraud the organisation.
items.note: Formal verb: defraud someone of money or property.

items.example: The abduction was reported to the authorities immediately.
items.note: Taking someone away illegally, particularly a child in the source explanation.

items.example: Witnesses gave a description of the suspected abductor.
items.note: Person noun from abduct.

items.example: Investigators believed the child had been abducted.
items.note: Formal verb; abduct and kidnap overlap, but abduction need not involve ransom.

items.example: He was accused of committing a crime during the protest.
items.note: The natural collocation is commit a crime, not make a crime.

items.example: Two armed men attempted to rob a bank outside the town.
items.note: Rob takes the person or place as object: rob a bank; steal money from a bank.

items.example: The police investigated the robbery of a local bank.
items.note: A crime involving taking property by force or threat, distinct from burglary.

items.example: A taxi driver witnessed the crime and called the police.
items.note: Witness can be a verb meaning see an event happen and also a noun for someone who saw it.

items.example: Officers arrested the suspect after questioning several witnesses.
items.note: A police action; arrest does not mean that a person has been convicted.

items.pt: acusar formalmente alguém de um crime
items.example: Police charged the driver with dangerous driving.
items.note: Fixed legal pattern: charge someone with an offence.

items.example: The witness accused the man of taking the missing equipment.
items.note: Fixed pattern accuse someone of something or of doing something. An accusation is not a conviction.

items.example: The investigation suggested that the thief had an accomplice.
items.note: Someone who helps another person commit a crime.

items.example: A specialist team was asked to investigate the case.
items.note: Case is an incident or allegation under investigation; investigate can also take a crime as its object.

items.example: The detective reopened the case after receiving new evidence.
items.note: Here, a particular crime or legal matter; case has many other meanings.

items.example: Investigators continued to collect evidence at the scene.
items.note: Evidence is normally uncountable: some evidence, a piece of evidence; not an evidence.

items.example: The evidence was examined before the trial began.
items.note: Uncountable noun. Evidence can support a conclusion without establishing it conclusively.

items.pt: cena do crime; local do crime
items.example: Technicians photographed the crime scene before moving anything.
items.note: The place where a crime happened or where evidence is sought.

items.example: Police compared the fingerprints with their records.
items.note: Marks from fingers that may help identify people; plural is common.

items.example: DNA evidence helped investigators identify the unknown person.
items.note: Biological evidence analysed for genetic information; DNA is spoken as letter names.

items.example: The phone records helped link the suspect to the crime.
items.note: Evidence may establish an association; that alone does not necessarily prove guilt.

items.example: The investigator said there was not yet enough proof of the claim.
items.note: The textbook distinguishes proof as conclusive support from evidence as material used to establish facts.

items.example: The court found the defendant guilty of the offence.
items.note: Common legal pattern found guilty of; contrast with innocent.

items.example: Police questioned a suspect near the station.
items.note: The noun has first-syllable stress /ˈsʌspekt/; the verb usually /səˈspekt/.

items.pt: ser levado à Justiça; chegar ao tribunal
items.example: The case may come to court later this year.
items.note: The source uses come to court when a legal case reaches a trial or hearing.

items.example: The lawyer presented the documents to the court.
items.note: An institution or place where legal cases are decided.

items.example: The two defendants were tried in the same court.
items.note: Passive of try in the legal sense: to examine a case and decide guilt.

items.example: The trial continued for another three days.
items.note: The legal proceedings in which the evidence is considered.

items.example: The defendant chose to plead not guilty at the hearing.
items.note: Legal expression: plead guilty or plead not guilty; past pleaded is standard.

items.example: The defendant decided to plead guilty to the charge.
items.note: The contrasting legal plea; note plead guilty to a charge.

items.example: Her lawyer requested additional time to review the evidence.
items.note: A professional who gives legal advice or represents someone; the book contrasts defence and prosecution roles.

items.example: A legal team was appointed to defend the accused.
items.note: In legal contexts, represent or argue in favour of a person facing an accusation.

items.pt: advogado de acusação; membro da promotoria
items.example: The prosecuting lawyer questioned the main witness.
items.note: A lawyer arguing the case against the accused on behalf of the prosecution.

items.pt: apresentar uma argumentação ou conjunto de provas sólido
items.example: The prosecution tried to produce a strong case against the accused.
items.note: Here case means a body of arguments and evidence, rather than the whole legal procedure.

items.example: The jury reached its decision after lengthy deliberations.
items.note: Discussions held to consider a decision, especially by a jury.

items.example: The jury listened carefully to the final arguments.
items.note: A group of citizens tasked with deciding a verdict in certain types of trial.

items.pt: proferir um veredicto; dar um veredicto
items.example: The jury was ready to pass a verdict at the end of the trial.
items.note: The textbook also uses pass a verdict of guilty on someone.

items.example: The verdict was announced shortly after midday.
items.note: The formal decision on guilt or another issue at trial.

items.example: The court convicted the man of fraud.
items.note: Fixed pattern: be convicted of a crime; contrasts with being merely accused or charged.

items.example: She insisted that she was innocent of the allegations.
items.note: Not guilty of a crime; legally, a not-guilty verdict is not necessarily a proof of factual innocence.

items.example: The judge acquitted the defendant of the charge.
items.note: Fixed pattern: acquit someone of a charge or offence.

items.example: The judge explained the decision in court.
items.note: The person who presides over judicial proceedings and, in the source example, decides the sentence.

items.pt: sentenciar alguém a; condenar alguém a uma pena
items.example: The judge sentenced the offender to two years in prison.
items.note: Fixed pattern sentence someone to a punishment or term of imprisonment.

items.example: The court imposed a prison sentence for the offence.
items.note: The punishment of serving a specified time in prison.

items.example: The driver had to pay a fine for the offence.
items.note: A financial penalty imposed for breaking a rule or law; here a noun.

items.example: The offender will serve a prison sentence after the appeal.
items.note: Serve refers to spending the required time in prison.

items.pt: ser libertado da prisão; sair da prisão
items.example: He was released from prison after completing his sentence.
items.note: Release is distinct from acquit: a person may be released after serving a sentence.

items.pt: redução da pena por bom comportamento
items.example: The prisoner hoped to receive time off for good behaviour.
items.note: The phrase describes a reduction in time served; the legal rules vary by country.

items.example: The judge considered the appropriate punishment under the law.
items.note: A consequence imposed for an offence.

items.example: The programme offers support to young offenders.
items.note: A person who commits an offence; the related noun offence means an illegal act.

items.example: The court considered whether a criminal offence had occurred.
items.note: British spelling offence; American spelling offense.

items.example: The victim received support after reporting the incident.
items.note: The person harmed or affected by a crime.

items.example: A witness described the car leaving the building.
items.note: As a noun, someone who sees an event; witness is also a verb.

items.example: The accused was represented by two lawyers.
items.note: Person or people charged with a crime; not a synonym for convicted person.

items.example: The police suspected the employee of taking the missing files.
items.note: Pattern: suspect someone of doing something.

items.example: The complaint remains under investigation.
items.note: Expression practised in the exercise for a case still being examined.

items.example: The former official is on trial for fraud.
items.note: Expression for a person who is currently undergoing a trial.

sectionsChecked: A: Crimes, criminal labels and matching verb forms
B: Investigations, arrest, legal charges, evidence and DNA
C: Trials, verdicts, sentences and release
D: Crime-related roles and legal terminology
Exercises 39.1–39.4, including prepositions and relevant answer-key entries

units.title: Unit 40 — Money
units.source: Vocabulary study targets from published reference material; Unit 40. Page information, if available, is retained in sourceAudit.
units.category: Banking, personal finance, borrowing and taxation
learningObjectives: Describe banking products, accounts, borrowing, interest rates and repayments in natural British English.
Distinguish income, outgoings, debt, debit, credit, overdrafts and bank-account balances.
Use financial verb–noun patterns such as raise money, consolidate debts, transfer money and charge interest.
Identify the types of taxes and public-finance terminology presented in the source.

items.example: Learning about personal finance helped her plan her monthly budget.
items.note: Managing an individual's money, accounts, borrowing and savings.

items.example: My salary is paid directly into my current account.
items.note: British English bank account used for everyday transactions; commonly checking account in US English.

items.example: The bank increased the interest rate on its loans.
items.note: A percentage paid on savings or charged for borrowing, depending on the product.

items.example: He used his overdraft to cover an unexpected expense.
items.note: When spending exceeds the money available in a current account; charges may apply.

items.pt: limite de cheque especial; possibilidade de usar saldo negativo
items.example: The bank offered a small overdraft facility with the account.
items.note: Permission from a bank to overdraw up to an agreed amount.

items.example: She visited a bank branch to discuss her mortgage.
items.note: A physical office of a bank; the advertisements use branch.

items.example: They applied for a loan to replace their car.
items.note: Money borrowed with the obligation to repay it, often with interest.

items.example: The group organised an event to raise money for repairs.
items.note: Obtain money for a purpose; not the same as borrow money, which creates a debt.

items.example: Several lenders advertised competitive interest rates.
items.note: Rates advertised as comparable to or better than those of competitors.

items.example: She paid the hotel bill with a credit card.
items.note: A card that permits borrowing up to a set limit.

items.pt: consolidar dívidas; reunir dívidas em uma só
items.example: He explored whether to consolidate debts into a single loan.
items.note: Combining several debts or repayments; it does not necessarily reduce the total cost.

items.example: Paying off high-interest debt was her main financial priority.
items.note: Money owed; the b is silent. Distinguish debt from debit.

items.example: The next payment is due on Friday.
items.note: The act of paying or an amount paid.

items.example: He requested a higher credit limit on his card.
items.note: Maximum amount that may be borrowed or spent using a credit facility.

items.pt: financiamento imobiliário; empréstimo com garantia de imóvel
items.example: The couple compared mortgage offers before buying a flat.
items.note: A loan secured on property, typically used to buy a home.

items.example: They saved enough money for a deposit on a flat.
items.note: In this section, money paid upfront towards a purchase; deposit has other banking meanings.

items.pt: parcela de amortização; pagamento de dívida
items.example: Her monthly repayment remained the same throughout the year.
items.note: Money paid back to reduce a loan or other debt; plural repayments is common.

items.example: The loan advert promised flexible repayments.
items.note: Repayments whose timing or amount can be varied under agreed conditions.

items.example: The company decided to consolidate several small contracts.
items.note: General verb meaning combine into one; for finances, consolidate debts.

items.example: They needed a way to finance their trip.
items.note: Verb: provide or obtain the money needed for a purchase or activity.

items.example: A steady income made it easier to plan her expenses.
items.note: Money received regularly at a relatively predictable level.

items.example: The application asks for details of your monthly income.
items.note: Money coming in from work, investments or other sources; contrast with outgoings.

items.example: Rent and transport account for most of his monthly outgoings.
items.note: Money going out regularly; normally plural in this financial sense.

items.example: Moving house caused several major expenses.
items.note: Large costs, as opposed to smaller daily purchases.

items.example: The electricity bill is paid by direct debit.
items.note: A payment arrangement in which an organisation takes an agreed payment from your account.

items.example: The bank will debit your account for the subscription fee.
items.note: Debit means take money from an account; contrast with credit money to an account.

items.example: The company will credit your account with the refund.
items.note: In this context, add money to an account.

items.pt: avaliação de crédito; classificação de risco de crédito
items.example: A poor credit rating may make borrowing more expensive.
items.note: An assessment of creditworthiness; the exact scoring system depends on the country.

items.example: She decided to borrow money for the repairs.
items.note: Borrow something from someone; the borrower receives money and owes repayment.

items.pt: conta poupança; conta de aplicação para guardar dinheiro
items.example: He transfers part of his salary into a savings account.
items.note: An account for money not needed immediately; not necessarily the Brazilian regulated poupança product.

items.example: You can transfer money between your accounts online.
items.note: Common pattern transfer money from one account to another.

items.pt: com saldo positivo; com crédito na conta
items.example: My current account was still in credit at the end of the month.
items.note: A bank account has a positive balance; different from having a good credit rating.

items.pt: com saldo negativo; usando cheque especial
items.example: Her account became overdrawn after the rent payment.
items.note: An account has a negative balance; compare overdraft.

items.example: The business was in the red for several months.
items.note: Informal expression for owing more or having a negative balance.

items.example: Some banks charge interest on an overdraft.
items.note: Banks charge interest when lending; they may pay interest on savings.

items.example: His bank warned him that he had exceeded his overdraft limit.
items.note: The maximum authorised amount by which an account may be overdrawn.

items.pt: serviços bancários online; banco pela internet
items.example: Online banking allows her to pay bills without visiting a branch.
items.note: Using banking services through an internet-connected system.

items.example: He withdrew cash from a cash machine near the station.
items.note: British English term; ATM is also widely used.

items.example: She uses her phone to pay bills at the start of each month.
items.note: A common verb–noun collocation in personal finance.

items.example: The lecture examined the role of taxes in public finance.
items.note: Government revenue, spending and related financial activities.

items.example: The government introduced a new tax on the product.
items.note: A compulsory payment to public authorities; forms include income tax and VAT.

items.example: Income tax is deducted from many employees' wages.
items.note: Tax on income, including earnings from employment.

items.example: The family asked for advice about inheritance tax.
items.note: Tax related to assets received after a person's death; rules differ by jurisdiction.

items.pt: imposto ou tarifa de importação; tributo aduaneiro
items.example: Importers may have to pay customs duty on goods entering a country.
items.note: A tax imposed on imported goods, according to the source.

items.example: Excise duty can apply to specific goods.
items.note: The book groups customs and excise duty together, but their legal application may differ.

items.example: She bought a gift at a duty-free shop before her flight.
items.note: An airport or border shop selling eligible goods without certain taxes.

items.example: VAT was included in the price of the equipment.
items.note: Value added tax, a consumption tax on many goods and services; British abbreviation commonly pronounced as one word.

items.example: The receipt showed the value added tax separately.
items.note: Full form of VAT; rules and rates vary by jurisdiction.

items.pt: imposto sobre o lucro das empresas
items.example: The company included corporation tax in its financial forecast.
items.note: Tax on corporate profits; the UK's terminology in the source.

items.example: The firm reported higher profits after reducing its costs.
items.note: Money a business makes after relevant costs are subtracted; plural is frequent in financial reports.

items.example: Many graduates remain in debt for several years.
items.note: A useful expansion of the exercise discussion of outstanding debts.

items.example: She plans to pay back the loan within two years.
items.note: Phrasal verb for returning borrowed money; common object pattern: pay the money back.

sectionsChecked: A: Bank advertisements, borrowing and mortgage terminology
B: Bank services, balances and common financial expressions
C: Public-finance taxes and revenue terms
